a: Speak to the heart of Jerusalem
p: The Greek begins 40:2 "Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem", naming who is told to comfort.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), 1QIsa-b and 4QIsa-b (4Q56) agree
readings.en: speak to the heart of Jerusalem
readings.plain: Speak to the heart of Jerusalem

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.orig: ἱερεῖς, λαλήσατε εἰς τὴν καρδίαν Ἰερουσαλήμ
readings.en: priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem
readings.plain: Priests, speak to the heart of Jerusalem

why: Every Hebrew witness lacks "priests". The Greek translator, or the Hebrew copy he used, seems to have answered the question 40:1 leaves open: who are the plural "you" told to comfort? The Targum answers it differently ("prophets").

a: and all flesh will see it, all together
p: The Greek reads "all flesh will see the salvation of God". Luke 3:6 quotes it in that form.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) and 1QIsa-b agree
readings.en: and all flesh will see together
readings.plain: and all flesh will see it, all together

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s); Luke 3:6
readings.orig: καὶ ὄψεται πᾶσα σὰρξ τὸ σωτήριον τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.en: and all flesh will see the salvation of God
readings.plain: and all flesh will see God's salvation

why: The Hebrew is shorter and supported by both Qumran scrolls. The Greek supplies an object for "see", perhaps from 52:10, where every far end of the earth "will see how our God saves".
b: Luke follows the Greek when he quotes 40:3–5 for John the Baptist (Luke 3:4–6).

a: I answered
p: The scroll and the Greek have the prophet answer: "And I said". The Masoretic vowels read "And he said".

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (ואומרה); Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s); Vulgate
readings.en: and I said
readings.plain: I answered

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (its consonants allow either; the vowels make it third person); KJV
readings.en: and he said
readings.plain: Someone answered

why: Two old witnesses, in Hebrew and Greek, have the first person, and the Masoretic consonants can be read the same way (va'omar). The answer "What am I to call out?" fits a prophet being called, as in 6:8–11. Most modern translations follow the scroll and the Greek here.
b: If the Masoretic vowels are followed, a second heavenly voice answers the first, and the prophet is not named. On the call, see the note.

a: all its loyal love
p: The Greek has "all the glory of man". 1 Peter 1:24 quotes the Greek: "all its glory".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (חַסְדּוֹ); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) has the plural, "its loyal deeds" (חסדיו)
readings.en: and all its loyal love
readings.plain: all its loyal love

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s); 1 Peter 1:24
readings.en: and all the glory of man
readings.plain: all human glory

why: The Hebrew word is chesed, unexpected here, which is why the Greek and many modern translations smooth it to "glory" or "beauty". The harder Hebrew word is kept, with the note explaining it.

a: for the LORD's wind has blown on it. / Yes, the people are grass.
p: Goes with 40:8. The Greek and the scroll's first scribe lack these lines and the first line of 40:8.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); added in Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) by a later corrector
readings.orig: כִּי רוּחַ יְהוָה נָשְׁבָה בּוֹ אָכֵן חָצִיר הָעָם
readings.en: for the breath of YHWH has blown on it; surely the people are grass
readings.plain: for the LORD's wind has blown on it. / Yes, the people are grass.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), first hand; Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s); 1 Peter 1:24–25
readings.en: (lacking)

why: The full text is the Masoretic one and is in all later Hebrew copies. The short text most likely arose when a copyist's eye jumped from the first "The grass dries up, the flower wilts" (40:7) to the second (40:8), so that everything between dropped out; the Greek translator's Hebrew copy probably had the same gap. Some scholars think instead that the short text is older and 40:7b–8a an early expansion.
b: In the Great Isaiah Scroll the missing words were added between the lines and down the margin by a later hand, which also wrote the divine name as four small strokes, like the letter yod. 1 Peter 1:24–25 quotes the short Greek form.

a: The grass dries up, the flower wilts,
p: Goes with 40:7. Without this line, the Greek and the scroll's first scribe read 40:7a + 40:8b.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); added in Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) by a later corrector
readings.en: grass withers, flower fades
readings.plain: The grass dries up, the flower wilts,

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), first hand; Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s); 1 Peter 1:24–25
readings.en: (lacking)

why: See the variant on 40:7: the repeated line is where a copyist's eye most easily skipped.

a: Who has held the waters in his palm to measure them,
t: "The waters" or "the waters of the sea"
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "the waters of the sea". The Masoretic Text and the Greek have "the waters".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.en: waters
readings.plain: Who has held the waters in his palm to measure them,

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: the waters of the sea
readings.plain: Who has held the waters of the sea in his palm to measure them,

why: The shorter reading has the Masoretic Text and the Greek behind it. The scroll's "sea" makes the picture explicit and may be a scribe's addition; the meaning is the same.

a: Who has taken the measure of the LORD's Spirit?
p: The Greek reads "Who knew the Lord's mind?" Paul quotes it in Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) agrees
readings.en: who has measured the spirit of YHWH?
readings.plain: Who has taken the measure of the LORD's Spirit?

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s); Romans 11:34; 1 Corinthians 2:16
readings.en: who knew the mind of the Lord?
readings.plain: Who knew the Lord's mind?

why: The Hebrew verb tikken is the measuring verb of 40:12, which ties the verse to the questions before it. The Greek gives the sense rather than the picture.

a: so that we stare at each other / and see it all together
p: The written Hebrew can be read "and be afraid"; the read text has "and see". The scroll has "hear" for "stare".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read text (Qere); 1QIsa-b
readings.en: that we may look at one another and see together
readings.plain: so that we stare at each other / and see it all together

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv) ונרא, read venira', a form of "fear"
readings.en: that we may be dismayed and be afraid together
readings.plain: so that we are dismayed / and afraid together

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: that we may hear and see together
readings.plain: so that we hear / and see it all together

why: The read text (Qere) is supported by 1QIsa-a's "and see", and the pairing "stare" and "see" is natural. The rare verb nishta'ah ("look at each other" or "be dismayed", as in 41:10) is the harder reading; the scroll replaces it with the common "hear".
b: The KJV's "that we may be dismayed, and behold it together" takes the first verb as "be dismayed" and follows the read text for the second.

a: and your work from nothingness
p: The Masoretic word me'afa' occurs only here. 1QIsa-b has me'efes, "from nothing"; the Greek "from earth".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (מֵאָפַע, usually taken as a slip for מֵאֶפֶס); 1QIsa-b (1Q8, late first century BC) (מאפס)
readings.en: and your work [is] from nothing
readings.plain: and your work from nothingness

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.orig: πόθεν ἡ ἐργασία ὑμῶν; ἐκ γῆς
readings.en: where does your work come from? From the earth
readings.plain: and your work from the earth

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (lacks the word)
readings.en: and your work
readings.plain: and your work

why: 1QIsa-b confirms the meaning most translators give the Masoretic word: 'efes, "nothing", as in 41:12 and 41:29. The Plain follows that sense.

a: he will call on my name
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "by his name"; the Greek "they will be called by my name".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: he will call on my name
readings.plain: he will call on my name

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (ויקרא בשמו)
readings.en: and he will call (or: be called) by his name
readings.plain: he will be called by his name

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.en: they will be called by my name
readings.plain: they will be called by my name

why: The Masoretic "my name" is supported by the Greek. The scroll's "his name" removes the difficulty that Cyrus, according to 45:4–5, did not know the LORD, and may be an easier reading influenced by 45:3–4, where God calls Cyrus by name. Some scholars prefer it.
b: If the scroll is followed, the line means that God summons Cyrus by name, as in 45:3–4, rather than that Cyrus worships the LORD. See the note.

a: a fraud!
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "nothing" ('ayin) for "a fraud" ('aven). The Greek paraphrases the verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.en: wickedness, delusion
readings.plain: a fraud!

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (אין)
readings.en: nothing
readings.plain: nothing!

why: The two words differ by one letter. The Masoretic "fraud" fits the charge against the gods; the scroll's "nothing" repeats 41:24 ("you come from nothing"), and some modern versions follow it. The Greek, "for those who make you are..., and in vain those who lead you astray", is too free to decide.

a: Look at my servant!
p: The Greek names the servant: "Jacob my servant ... Israel my chosen". No Hebrew witness has the names.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) agrees
readings.en: here is my servant
readings.plain: Look at my servant!

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.orig: Ἰακὼβ ὁ παῖς μου ... Ἰσραὴλ ὁ ἐκλεκτός μου
readings.en: Jacob my servant ... Israel my chosen
readings.plain: Jacob is my servant!

why: The Hebrew does not name the servant here, and the Greek names look like an interpretation drawn from 41:8 and 44:1. Matthew 12:18, which quotes the song for Jesus, does not have them.
b: The Greek identification with Israel is one side of the long debate on the servant's identity: see the note and the chapter page.

a: The islands are waiting for his teaching.
t: "In his name the nations will hope"
p: The Greek reads "and nations will hope in his name". Matthew 12:21 quotes that form.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 4Q56 and 4Q62 (4QIsa-h) agree where preserved
readings.en: and for his teaching the islands wait
readings.plain: The islands are waiting for his teaching.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s); Matthew 12:21
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ ὀνόματι αὐτοῦ ἔθνη ἐλπιοῦσιν
readings.en: and in his name nations will hope
readings.plain: The nations will hope in his name.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (ינחילו)
readings.en: and the islands will inherit his teachings
readings.plain: The islands will inherit his teachings.

why: The Masoretic reading has two Qumran fragments beside it for "his teaching". The Greek is a free rendering that Matthew follows; the Great Isaiah Scroll's verb differs by one letter and is probably a copying slip.

a: You are my witnesses, the LORD declares,
p: The Greek reads "Be my witnesses, and I too am a witness, says the Lord God".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) and 1QIsa-b agree
readings.en: you are my witnesses, declares YHWH
readings.plain: You are my witnesses, the LORD declares,

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.orig: γένεσθέ μοι μάρτυρες, κἀγὼ μάρτυς, λέγει κύριος ὁ θεός
readings.en: become my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God
readings.plain: Be my witnesses, and I too am a witness, the Lord God declares,

why: All the Hebrew witnesses have the shorter text. The Greek plus makes God a witness in his own trial, an idea found in Jeremiah 29:23 and Malachi 3:5.

a: and rivers in the barren land.
p: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads "paths in the barren land", matching "road". The Masoretic Text and the Greek have "rivers".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.en: rivers in the desert
readings.plain: and rivers in the barren land.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC)
readings.en: paths in the desert
readings.plain: and paths in the barren land.

why: "Rivers in the barren land" is repeated in 43:20 and is backed by the Greek. The scroll's "paths" makes a neater pair with "road" and is probably a scribe's smoothing. 4QIsa-g (4Q61) is broken at this word and cannot decide.

a: Israel, you will not be forgotten by me.
p: The Greek reads "Israel, do not forget me". The Great Isaiah Scroll has a different verb.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); 1QIsa-b and 4Q56 agree
readings.en: you will not be forgotten by me
readings.plain: Israel, you will not be forgotten by me.

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.en: do not forget me
readings.plain: Israel, do not forget me.

readings.w: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) (תשאני)
readings.en: you will not deceive me (or: forget me)
readings.plain: Israel, do not deceive me.

why: Two Qumran copies support the Masoretic form, which is unusual but clear (see the note). The Greek and the Great Isaiah Scroll read an easier active verb.

a: (who was with me?)
p: The written Hebrew, with two Qumran scrolls and the Greek, asks "who?". The read text has "by myself".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), written text (Ketiv); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) and 4Q56
readings.en: who was with me?
readings.plain: (who was with me?)

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), read text (Qere); KJV
readings.en: from with me, by myself
readings.plain: by myself

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s) (joins the question to 44:25)
readings.en: who else? (beginning 44:25: "Who else will scatter the signs...?")
readings.plain: (who else?)

why: The written text has the support of the Great Isaiah Scroll and 4Q56, both of which write "who" as a separate word, and, in its own way, of the Greek, which read the same "who?" and joined it to the next verse. Its sharp question matches the challenges of 40:13–14 and 44:7. The read text gives the same sense as a statement.
b: Modern translations divide: some follow the written text ("Who was with me?"), others the read text ("by myself").

a: and of the towns of Judah
p: In Codex Vaticanus, as Swete prints it, the Greek has "the cities of Idumea" (Edom) for "the towns of Judah".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC), 1QIsa-b and 4Q56 agree
readings.en: and of the cities of Judah
readings.plain: and of the towns of Judah

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (AD 300s), as printed by Swete
readings.en: and to the cities of Idumea
readings.plain: and of the towns of Edom

why: The Greek names Ioudaia and Idoumaia look alike, and the reading is almost certainly a copying slip within the Greek tradition; every Hebrew witness has Judah.

a: My shepherd!
p: The Greek reads "who tells Cyrus to be wise". The Hebrew consonants are read differently.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) and 1QIsa-b agree
readings.en: my shepherd
readings.plain: My shepherd!

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.en: to be wise (to think rightly)
readings.plain: Be wise!

why: All the Hebrew witnesses have ro'i, "my shepherd", and the royal title fits 45:1, where Cyrus is called the LORD's anointed. The Greek translator seems to have taken the word from an Aramaic verb meaning "think, will".

a: and to the temple, "You will have your foundations laid."
p: The Greek reads "and I will lay the foundations of my holy house", with God speaking in the first person.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a, about 125 BC) and 4Q56 agree
readings.en: and the temple, it will be founded
readings.plain: and to the temple, "You will have your foundations laid."

readings.w: Old Greek (Septuagint, 100s BC; Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, AD 300s)
readings.orig: καὶ τὸν οἶκον τὸν ἅγιόν μου θεμελιώσω
readings.en: and I will found my holy house
readings.plain: and "I will lay the foundations of my holy house."

why: The Hebrew witnesses agree. The Greek turns the line into a promise in God's own voice, perhaps to avoid having God address a building.
